title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract Reverse and forward Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student’s active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Earlier knowledge distillation methods use KL divergences to transfer predictive structure from a teacher to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . Adaptive KL (AKL) adjusts the early-training balance between forward and reverse KL according to distributional gaps within teacher-defined high-probability head and long-tail regions ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student at its own generated prefixes, where a frozen teacher provides supervision for the same next-token decision ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Agarwal et al., 2024b ) . At each prefix, the aligned student distribution q q and teacher distribution p p define two complementary objectives. Reverse KL (RKL), D KL ( q ∥ p ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p) , is associated with mode-seeking refinement of student-supported candidates, while forward KL (FKL), D KL ( p ∥ q ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q) , provides mode-covering supervision toward teacher-supported alternatives ( Agarwal et al., 2024b ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . As the student changes, so do the visited prefixes and the conditional predictions of both models. How should these corrections be coordinated within one update at the current teacher–student state? Recent OPD methods adapt supervision using uncertainty, token importance, teacher–student mismatch, and divergence routing ( Ko et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . At a visited prefix, two aspects of the predictive state inform this adaptation: each model’s self-uncertainty and the disagreement between their predictions. Self-uncertainty describes the dispersion of a model’s candidate probabilities; disagreement describes the mismatch requiring correction. Connecting these quantities to the two KL gradients provides a state-dependent basis for their relative influence and joint improvement. We place these signals in a common source–evaluator system: the student and teacher each supply candidate mass, and either model can evaluate it. The resulting four-observation matrix separates self-uncertainty, represented by its diagonal entropies, from directed disagreement, recovered by centering its cross-entropies on the corresponding source entropies. These contrasts yield the refinement and coverage objectives at the same student-visited state. This representation also links observations to correction geometry. For positive p , q p,q , the reverse- and forward-KL logit gradients satisfy g R ⊤ J ( q ) + g F = D KL ( q ∥ p ) + D KL ( p ∥ q ) g_{R}^{\top}J(q)^{+}g_{F}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q) , where J ⁡ ( q ) J(q) is the categorical Fisher matrix. For p ≠ q p\neq q , this positive cross-observation excess establishes a common local descent direction for both KL objectives in student-logit space. We develop observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) by connecting the observed teaching state to three decisions: preference , direction , and strength . Self-entropies set preferences between the two corrections, a closed-form bargaining solution coordinates their normalized gradients within the common-descent region, and symmetric distributional discrepancy scales supervision strength. These components connect self-uncertainty, correction geometry, and disagreement in a single bounded logit update, applied with one student backward pass. Figure 1 summarizes the observation → \rightarrow contrast → \rightarrow coordination → \rightarrow strength pipeline. We evaluate OC-OPD on mathematical reasoning in three Qwen3 student settings ( Qwen Team, 2025c ) , all trained with fresh student rollouts: non-thinking students at 1.7B and 4B scales, thinking-generation students, and a weaker base-model initialization. In the main non-thinking setting, the 1.7B student exceeds the strongest compared baseline by + 6.88 +6.88 Avg@32 and + 11.11 +11.11 Pass@32 points on average across AIME24–26; the 4B student exceeds EOPD ( Jin et al., 2026 ) by + 2.74 +2.74 and + 3.33 +3.33 points, respectively (Table 1 ). Gains persist in the other two settings, and GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2023 ) and MBPP+ ( Liu et al., 2023 ) assess transfer to scientific question answering and code generation. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We unifiedly describe token-level OPD through a source–evaluator system whose self- and cross-observations characterize the teaching state and whose source-centered contrasts recover the two KL corrections. (2) We prove a Fisher inverse-metric identity linking those contrasts to their logit gradients and establish common local descent for every distinct positive teacher–student pair. (3) We develop OC-OPD to determine the preference, direction, and strength of token-level supervision, and demonstrate its effectiveness across heterogeneous student settings and out-of-domain evaluations.

sections.heading: KL directions in on-policy distillation.
sections.text: Earlier knowledge distillation methods transfer predictive structure from a teacher to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . AKL adaptively combines forward and reverse KL using distributional gaps within teacher-defined head and tail regions, motivated by their different fitting priorities in early training ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . A larger head gap increases the forward-KL weight, while a larger tail gap increases the reverse-KL weight. OPD evaluates teacher guidance at student-generated prefixes ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Agarwal et al., 2024b ) , where both models produce aligned next-token distributions. GKD studies flexible divergence objectives at these states ( Agarwal et al., 2024b ) , and MiniLLM develops reverse-KL distillation under student sampling ( Gu et al., 2024 ) . Related methods explore skewed divergences and adaptive sampling ( Ko et al., 2024 ) , contrastive teacher–student responses ( Ko et al., 2025 ) , and interleaved generation ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Reverse KL refines relative probabilities among student-supported candidates, while forward KL transfers mass toward teacher-supported candidates. EOPD conditions forward-KL supervision on teacher entropy ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , and SEAD adjusts the emphasis of the two KL directions across tokens ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . We study how the current teacher–student state relates to these corrections: source-centering separates self-uncertainty from directed disagreement, and an exact observation–gradient identity establishes their joint local compatibility.

sections.heading: Observation-based adaptive supervision.
sections.text: At a shared prefix, either model can supply candidate mass and either model can evaluate it. These choices produce four observations: two self-entropies describe the predictive states of the student and teacher, and two cross-entropies combine source uncertainty with directed cross-model disagreement. Related methods use local information to determine how supervision is assigned. REOPOLD uses entropy-based token selection and relaxed reward shaping ( Ko et al., 2026 ) ; SMOPD selects informative positions for self-distillation ( Jiang and Huang, 2026 ) ; TIP combines student uncertainty with divergence to assess token importance ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , while TIDE characterizes student-excess and student-deficit mismatch ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Region-dependent objectives, adaptive targets, bounded transformations, and trust-region control further shape local supervision ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Jang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Xing et al., 2026 ) . Our source–evaluator matrix connects these signals through the entropy decomposition of KL: source-centering isolates the two directed disagreements, whose gradients supply the refinement and coverage corrections. Self-entropies set their relative preferences, gradient geometry coordinates their direction, and distributional discrepancy sets supervision strength. Appendix G summarizes representative methods in this notation.

sections.heading: Gradient coordination.
sections.text: Multi-objective optimization derives shared update directions via minimum-norm descent, gradient projection, conflict-averse optimization, and bargaining. Our KL gradients stem from aligned student–teacher distributions and source-centered observation contrasts, whose local coupling follows an exact Fisher-geometric identity. We leverage this identity to coordinate candidate-level refinement and coverage, adopting bargaining to obtain an observation-conditioned closed-form update direction. Scalarization and normalized gradient mixing serve as baselines for comparison.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries and Motivation
sections.text: This section formalizes shared-context OPD, organizes the aligned student and teacher distributions into four observations, and shows how their source-centered contrasts recover the ranking and coverage signals of reverse and forward KL.

sections.heading: Student-sourced contrast: rank and refine active support.
sections.text: For reverse KL, the token-level credit A i = log ⁡ ( p i / q i ) A_{i}=\log(p_{i}/q_{i}) compares teacher support with the student’s current allocation. Since A i > A j A_{i}>A_{j} exactly when p i / q i > p j / q j p_{i}/q_{i}>p_{j}/q_{j} , this credit ranks student-supported candidates by relative underallocation. The student-sourced contrast thereby refines the alternatives the student already explores. Its logit gradient is weighted by q i q_{i} , concentrating the correction on candidates that carry student probability.

sections.heading: Teacher-sourced contrast: recover underrepresented support.
sections.text: Forward KL evaluates teacher-sourced candidates under the student. Its logit gradient q − p q-p directly reallocates mass toward teacher-supported alternatives, including those with very small student probability. This coverage correction allocates student capacity across the teacher-supported set ( Gu et al., 2024 ) . In our full-vocabulary construction, the teacher-sourced gradient is evaluated directly at the visited prefix, yielding the exact candidate-level correction from the aligned distributions.

sections.heading: From complementary contrasts to a coordination problem.
sections.text: The matrix thus provides both statistics describing the current state and contrasts specifying candidate-level corrections. Existing entropy gates, token filters, and mismatch criteria can be interpreted as selecting or weighting particular regions of this object ( Ko et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Together, the source-centered contrasts invite a geometric account of when their ranking/refinement and coverage gradients share a descent direction. Section 4 establishes this compatibility; Section 5 uses self-observation, compatibility, and discrepancy to determine preference, direction, and magnitude.

sections.heading: 4 Theory: From Observations to Compatible Gradients
sections.text: The matrix view yields two source-centered corrections whose candidate-level gradients can be studied together. Their ranking/refinement and coverage directions admit common descent, with the observation matrix providing an explicit certificate of compatibility.

sections.heading: Models and training data.
sections.text: Students are Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, with Qwen3-4B-Base used for the base-initialization study ( Qwen Team, 2025c ) . We use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 as teachers ( Qwen Team, 2025a ; Qwen Team, 2025b ) . The main setting pairs the Instruct teacher with non-thinking students; auxiliary settings use the Thinking teacher with thinking students and the Instruct teacher with Qwen3-4B-Base. All methods train on DAPO-Math-17k ( Yu et al., 2025 ) with fresh student rollouts; distillation methods query a frozen teacher at the same student prefixes.

sections.heading: Evaluation benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate AIME24–26, MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) and OlympiadBench(math,english) ( He et al., 2024 ) for mathematical reasoning and GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2023 ) and MBPP+ ( Liu et al., 2023 ) for out-of-distribution transfer. Avg@32 is the mean accuracy over 32 responses per problem and Pass@32 the fraction of problems solved by at least one; OOD columns report Avg@32 in Table 1 and Pass@32 in Table 3 . Additional mathematical benchmarks are reported with Avg@8 or Pass@8 as indicated. Variance and statistical-significance analyses for the AIME evaluations are provided in Appendix J . We compare with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , OPD ( Agarwal et al., 2024a ) , OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) , EOPD ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , and KD ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , as applicable. The 4B non-thinking setting also reports pure RKL and FKL objectives. Within each comparison, methods share initialization, prompts, rollout budget, decoding, and evaluation protocol, and teacher-based methods share the same teacher.

sections.heading: Performance on mathematical reasoning.
sections.text: Table 1 shows consistent gains for both non-thinking student scales. For Qwen3-1.7B, OC-OPD outperforms GRPO, OPD, and OPSD on all six AIME metrics, beating the strongest baseline by +6.88 Avg@32 and +11.11 Pass@32 points on average. For Qwen3-4B, it exceeds EOPD by +2.74 Avg@32 and +3.33 Pass@32 points across AIME24–26. OC-OPD is best or tied-best in five of six columns, with RKL higher only on AIME24 Avg@32 by 0.10 points. Thus, the gains cover both average accuracy and multi-sample success.

sections.heading: Combining the two KL directions.
sections.text: Neither KL direction dominates at 4B: RKL leads FKL by 5.62 Avg@32 points on AIME24, whereas FKL is stronger on AIME25–26 and keeps MBPP+ at initialization. OC-OPD retains both strengths: it is within 0.10 points of RKL on AIME24, exceeds the stronger one by +2.92 and +4.37 Avg@32 points on AIME25–26, and surpasses both OOD. It also beats the adaptive linear mixture on all six AIME metrics (Table 4 ), so the gain comes from coordination rather than mixing alone.

sections.heading: Generalization beyond mathematical reasoning.
sections.text: Although trained only on DAPO-Math-17k, OC-OPD also improves out-of-distribution performance (Table 1 , last two columns). Relative to its initialization, the 1.7B student gains +4.42 points on GPQA-Diamond and +2.98 points on MBPP+. At 4B, it reaches 46.80 and 66.01, exceeding EOPD by +1.35 and +1.20 points. On MBPP+, OC-OPD stays above initialization, whereas EOPD and OPD (RKL) drop by 0.74 and 1.26 points.

sections.heading: Effect of individual design choices.
sections.text: Table 4 shows that no ablated objective matches the full OC-OPD across AIME24–26. RKL is only 0.10 points higher on AIME24 Avg@32, but is clearly worse on AIME25–26 and on Pass@32, while FKL shows a similar coverage gap. Adaptive linear mixing and equal-preference weighting recover part of the performance but remain below the full method. Removing the position gate is the strongest ablation, yet it reduces Pass@32 by about 3.33 points on all three benchmarks. These comparisons show that direction-aware preferences and position-sensitive weighting provide complementary benefits. Detailed definitions are given in Appendix I.4 ; the corresponding AIME results and statistical-analysis protocol are summarized in Appendix J .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: OC-OPD organizes teacher and student predictions at each student-generated prefix into four self- and cross-observations, yielding a unified supervision state. Source-centered contrasts recover the complementary ranking and coverage corrections of reverse and forward KL. The observation–gradient identity establishes their local compatibility, while observation-conditioned coordination combines them in a bounded update that retains a correction for teacher-supported candidates with low student probability. Experiments across non-thinking, thinking, and base-initialized students show consistent gains in mathematical reasoning. Scientific question answering and code generation further assess transfer beyond the mathematical training domain.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools were used solely for limited assistance with language polishing, formatting, routine coding, and debugging. The research, analysis, interpretation of results, and preparation of the final content were carried out by the human authors. All results and citations were independently verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the work.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work studies on-policy distillation using publicly available datasets and pre-trained open-source models, and all experiments follow the licenses of the corresponding resources. Because distillation can transfer characteristics of the teacher into the student, downstream use should include task-appropriate evaluation of factuality, bias, and safety together with standard deployment safeguards.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Full proofs appear in Appendices. Appendix H describes the gradient implementation, and Appendix I provides training and sampling hyperparameters, evaluation protocols, and controlled comparisons.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Near agreement, the two source-centered gradients agree to first order. Preference-dependent changes enter at higher order, and the gate controls the leading attenuation. Equation ( 37 ) quantifies the resulting cubic allocation of supervision to small discrepancies, including its slower fine-matching scale. A positive gate floor would restore a first-order term. The unit-gate ablation isolates the contribution of discrepancy-dependent attenuation.

Concentrated predictions with different favored candidates can have large Hellinger discrepancy and receive strong supervision. Position strength thus responds to cross-model mismatch, while self-observations condition the relative candidate-source influence.

sections.text: Teacher and student distributions share vocabulary semantics and next-token positions. Both models evaluate the exact student continuation. sections.heading: I.1 Models and experimental organization
sections.text: The teacher checkpoints are Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. The main experiment pairs the Instruct teacher with non-thinking Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B students. The first auxiliary experiment pairs the Thinking teacher with thinking students at both sizes; the second pairs the Instruct teacher with Qwen3-4B-Base. Within each comparison block, methods use the same student initialization, teacher, prompt source, training budget, generation/evaluation configuration, and metric implementation; only the learning objective or controller component being compared is changed. Each iteration generates fresh student continuations and aligns teacher and student distributions on the collected prefixes. The four observations, gradient geometry, and coefficients are recomputed at every valid response position. The teacher remains frozen, and the backward pass updates the student. The selected student regime determines the generation configuration of its training and evaluation continuations, and all methods in that regime use the same prompt wrapper and decoding protocol.
